The West Oakland Stabilization Fund was established in Cycle 78 when Mayor Avery Santana proposed and signed the initiative following a 6–3 City Council approval, dedicating a \$28 million allocation to shield multi-generational flatland residents and local businesses from displacement as industrial parcels gave way to waterfront developments (*bay_tribune_e83.pdf* [1-3]; *bay_tribune_e84.pdf* [4]; *The Balance on the Gavel: Avery Santana and the Architecture of Conditional Prosperity* [5]). Council President Ramon Vega voted in favor, Leonard Tran voted against, and Elliott Crane voted yes remotely (*cycle_pulse_c110.txt* [6]; *cycle_pulse_c111.txt* [7]; *cycle_pulse_c112.txt* [8]). Initial intake brought 342 applications—far exceeding the 150 projected—leaving the review team at the Office of Economic and Workforce Development overwhelmed and 295 households stalled in administrative limbo (*bay_tribune_e84.pdf* [129–130, 134]; *bay_tribune_e85.pdf* [9]).

To clear the processing stall, Mayor Santana reassigned direct disbursement oversight to Deputy Mayor Brenda Okoro under a 90-day consolidation cap, pairing her authority with Program Director Marcus Webb's intake desk (*bay_tribune_e90.pdf* [10, 11]; *bay_tribune_e91.pdf* [237–238]; *bay_tribune_e92.pdf* [268–269]). Webb accelerated reviews to roughly fifty applications per week, clearing an initial batch of 47 disbursements totaling \$4.2 million (*bay_tribune_e84.pdf* [12, 13]; *bay_tribune_e90.pdf* [10]). However, an executive signature chokepoint between Okoro’s office and the mayor's desk left 83 approved households backlogged, prompting Councilmember Warren Ashford to demand formal audits on disbursement velocity (*bay_tribune_e86.pdf* [14, 15]; *bay_tribune_e92.pdf* [267–270]; *bay_tribune_e93.pdf* [16]). Over a year into the program, only eighteen checks had cleared, forcing Mayor Santana to impose a get-well directive in Cycle 98 (*bay_tribune_e98.pdf* [335–338]).

By Cycle 110, Webb standardized reporting around an average 23-day processing window, executing regular \$400,000 monthly tranches that pushed cumulative spending past \$5 million by Cycle 112 (*cycle_pulse_c110.txt* [401–402]; *cycle_pulse_c111.txt* [413–416]; *cycle_pulse_c112.txt* [422, 430–432]). Behind that benchmark, Webb disclosed that six household files remained stalled awaiting title searches, where families faced eviction regardless of statistical averages (*cycle_pulse_c112.txt* [17, 18]). As outlays neared \$6.6 million in Cycle 114, construction trades and neighborhood workers warned that corporate tech expansions continued to drive displacement across West Oakland (*cycle_pulse_c114.corrected.txt* [458, 465–467]). Across each phase, public ledgers tracked aggregated dollar totals without naming individual recipients or addresses, leaving the gap between administrative throughput and street-level stability unresolved as the charter approached council renewal (*cycle_pulse_c108.txt* [378, 382–384]; *cycle_pulse_c109.txt* [386, 389–392]; *cycle_pulse_c111.txt* [413, 417–418]).
